Hydrangea radiata is a Southern Appalachian endemic closely related to smooth hydrangea (Hydrangea arborescens), distinguished by the brilliant silvery-white undersides of its leaves, which flash dramatically whenever the foliage moves in a breeze, topped by flattened clusters of small white flowers with a ring of showier sterile florets in summer. Its striking two-toned foliage effect makes it a distinctive choice for a shaded native shrub border, and its Appalachian mountain origin gives it good tolerance of the humid Southeast when given adequate shade and moisture. Prune out old wood in late winter as needed, since it blooms on new growth and tolerates hard pruning well if rejuvenation is needed.

directions: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; bracted hydrangea blooms later than most hydrangea species, from late summer into fall, avoiding damage from late spring frosts that can nip earlier bloomers. Hydrangea involucrata is a Japanese species notable for its unusual flower buds, which are wrapped in showy, papery bracts that peel back as the lacecap-form flower clusters of pale blue-lavender to pink open in late summer, later than nearly any other hydrangea. Its late bloom time and distinctive bud structure make it a valuable addition for extending hydrangea interest into fall in a shaded border, and it stays relatively compact compared with many other hydrangea species. Give it rich, evenly moist soil similar to bigleaf hydrangea, and protect from harsh winter cold at the northern edge of its hardiness range.

This dwarf, mounding selection of slender deutzia forms a low, wide mat of fine-textured, dark green foliage that turns burgundy-red in fall, smothered in a profusion of small, star-shaped white flowers in mid to late spring. Its low, spreading habit sets it apart from taller deutzia cultivars, making it well suited to a foundation planting, low informal hedge, or the front of a shrub border where a flowering groundcover effect is wanted. It tolerates part shade better than many flowering shrubs while still blooming well, and needs only light pruning after flowering to maintain a tidy shape.

directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Athens' is a yellow-flowered sport of native sweetshrub discovered in Georgia and is grown and cared for exactly like the wine-red species. Calycanthus floridus 'Athens' is a distinctive color break for the native sweetshrub, producing the same fruity, strawberry-banana-scented flowers as the typical maroon-red species but in a clear chartreuse-yellow, blooming over an extended period in late spring into early summer. Its unusual flower color and strong, sweet fragrance make it a good specimen for a shaded border or foundation planting near a patio or window where the scent can be enjoyed, and it shares the species' excellent shade tolerance and adaptability to a range of soils. Prune lightly after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on old wood and hard pruning will sacrifice the following year's flowers.

Vaccinium fuscatum is a tall, southeastern coastal-plain native blueberry with small, urn-shaped white to pink flowers in spring followed by sweet, dark purple-black berries in summer that are edible and attractive to wildlife, growing naturally in the moist, acidic soils of pocosins, bay forests, and wet flatwoods from the Carolinas to the Gulf Coast. Its tolerance for consistently damp soil and light shade makes it a good choice for a rain garden, pond margin, or the moist, partly shaded portion of a mixed berry planting where standard rabbiteye or southern highbush blueberries would struggle. It benefits from a second blueberry species or cultivar nearby for improved pollination and fruit set, following the same acidic-soil culture as other Vaccinium.
